documents.title: Mission and Theory of Change
documents.content:
# Harbor Light Health Collective — Mission and Theory of Change

Harbor Light Health Collective, Inc. is a 501(c)(3) public charity founded in 2013 and based in Oakland, California. Our programmes run across Alameda County, in Oakland, Berkeley, Hayward and San Leandro.

## Mission
Harbor Light Health Collective brings primary care, mental health care and practical support to unhoused and low-income adults in Alameda County, meeting people where they are.

## Theory of change
If unhoused and low-income adults receive primary and mental health care where they already are, and peer navigators with lived experience help them secure housing and benefits, then they will manage chronic conditions, rely less on emergency rooms and move toward stable housing. Trust built through repeated, low-barrier contact is what makes the clinical care stick.

## Principles
- Care is never conditional on sobriety or housing readiness.
- People with lived experience of homelessness shape our services, as staff and as board members.
- We measure clinical and housing outcomes for every patient.

documents.title: Programme Descriptions
documents.content:
# Programme Descriptions

## Street Medicine Van
A nurse practitioner, a medical assistant and a behavioural health clinician visit 14 regular stops in Oakland, Berkeley, Hayward and San Leandro, 5 days a week. Services include primary care, wound care, medication refills and brief counselling. 7,200 visits with 1,850 patients in 2025-26.

## Harbor Light Drop-In Clinic
A walk-in clinic on International Boulevard in East Oakland, open Monday to Friday, offering primary care, chronic disease management and counselling with no appointment needed. 11,400 visits with 2,610 patients in 2025-26.

## Peer Navigator Programme
12 peer navigators with lived experience of homelessness work alongside our clinicians, helping patients apply for Medi-Cal, CalFresh and disability benefits and secure interim or permanent housing. 1,480 patients worked with a navigator in 2025-26.

## Plans
- Add a second van in 2027 to reach southern Alameda County (about 900 more patients a year).
- Pilot a medical respite programme; no site chosen yet.

documents.title: 2025-26 Impact Report
documents.content:
# 2025-26 Impact Report

## Who we serve
- 3,940 unique patients received 18,600 visits (7,200 on the van, 11,400 at the clinic).
- 71% were unhoused at their first visit; 92% have incomes below 138% of the federal poverty level.
- 48% Black, 22% Latino/Hispanic, 17% white, 8% Asian/Pacific Islander, 5% Native American or multiracial.
- 41% report a disability; 38% have a serious mental illness diagnosis.

## Outcomes
- 418 patients moved into interim or permanent housing with a peer navigator's help.
- 1,290 patients were enrolled in Medi-Cal, CalFresh or disability benefits.
- 58% of patients with hypertension had blood pressure under 140/90 at their last visit, up from 44% in 2023-24.
- 62% of patients with moderate or severe depression (PHQ-9 of 10 or more) who attended three or more counselling visits improved by 5 points or more.
- Emergency room visits among navigated patients fell 31% in the six months after enrolment.

"The van came to me before I could come to anyone. Now I have a doctor and a key." — Patient, East Oakland

## How we measure
Clinical data: electronic health record. Housing and benefits data: navigator case-management database. Both reported quarterly.

documents.title: FY2026 Budget Summary
documents.content:
# FY2026 Budget Summary

Annual operating budget (FY2026, year ending June 30): $4.8 million.

## Expenses
- Clinical staff (physicians, nurse practitioners, nurses, medical assistants): $1,960,000
- Behavioural health clinicians: $720,000
- Peer navigators: $610,000
- Van operations, fuel, maintenance and medical supplies: $380,000
- Clinic rent and facilities: $290,000
- Data systems and electronic health record: $140,000
- Administration and finance: $450,000
- Fundraising: $250,000
- Total: $4,800,000

## Revenue mix
- Federal grants (direct federal health care for the homeless grant): 30%
- Medi-Cal reimbursement: 25%
- Foundations: 22%
- Alameda County contracts: 13%
- Individual donors: 7%
- Corporate gifts: 3%

Cost per patient: about $1,220 per year.

documents.title: Governance and Capacity
documents.content:
# Governance and Capacity

- Board of 11 directors; meets every other month. Three directors have lived experience of homelessness, and two are practising clinicians.
- Most recent audit: FY2025 independent audit, including a federal Single Audit, completed with a clean opinion and no findings.
- Staff: 38 full-time, 9 part-time, plus about 60 volunteer clinicians and health-professions students a year.
- We have managed a direct federal grant under Uniform Guidance since 2019.
- One full-time grants and compliance manager; the development director spends about 40% of time on grants.
- Policies in place: HIPAA privacy policy, conflict of interest policy, whistleblower policy, patient grievance policy, sliding fee scale policy, harm reduction policy.

## Key leaders
- Dr. Renata Okafor-Lisle, Executive Director — family physician; has led Harbor Light since 2017.
- Marcus Tanaka-Reyes, Director of Development — oversees fundraising and funder relationships.
- Priya Venkataraman, Grants and Compliance Manager — leads proposals, reporting and federal compliance.

documents.title: Organisation Overview
documents.content:
# Organisation Overview (approved language)

Harbor Light Health Collective brings primary care and mental health care to unhoused and low-income adults across Alameda County. Since 2013 we have met people where they are: on our Street Medicine Van, which visits 14 stops five days a week, and at our walk-in clinic in East Oakland. Twelve peer navigators with lived experience of homelessness help patients secure housing, Medi-Cal and other benefits. In 2025-26 we served 3,940 patients across 18,600 visits, and 418 patients moved into interim or permanent housing with a navigator's help. Care is never conditional on sobriety or housing readiness.

opportunities.raw_text:
Golden Coast Health Equity Fund — Community Clinic Access Grants (FICTIONAL SAMPLE)
The Fund invites California community clinics and safety-net providers to apply for one-year grants of $50,000 to $150,000 that expand access to primary care and behavioural health for low-income, uninsured and unhoused adults. Priority goes to organisations that deliver care outside traditional clinic walls, integrate mental health with primary care, and track clinical outcomes. Applicants must be 501(c)(3) organisations based in California with annual budgets between $1 million and $15 million. Funds may support staff, supplies, outreach and data systems; capital construction and hospital-based services are not eligible. Applications are due by 5:00 p.m. Pacific time on the deadline date and must include four narrative responses, a project budget with narrative, and the most recent audited financial statements. No match is required.

questions.prompt: Describe the need in your community and the population you will serve.
questions.answer: Harbor Light is the leading provider of street medicine in California and we are truly passionate about helping the most vulnerable people in our community. Every year we serve over 5,000 people, and nearly all of them are homeless. The need in Alameda County is huge and growing every day. Our van and clinic do amazing work and our patients really need us. With your support we can continue to make a real difference in so many lives.

Oakland Harbor Foundation — Behavioral Health Bridges (FICTIONAL SAMPLE)
Behavioral Health Bridges funds Alameda County nonprofits that help adults living with mental illness move from crisis or isolation into consistent care. We are especially interested in peer-led models, outreach to people experiencing homelessness, and programmes that link mental health care with housing and benefits. Grants range from $40,000 to $100,000 for one year. Inpatient psychiatric care and fundraising events are not eligible. Proposals must answer two narrative questions and include a programme budget and board list. Applications close at midnight on the published deadline. Grantees submit a final report with outcome data after 12 months.

questions.prompt: Describe the programme you are requesting support for and how it connects participants to ongoing care.
questions.answer: We request support for our Peer Navigator Programme. Twelve peer navigators with lived experience of homelessness work alongside our clinicians on the Street Medicine Van and at the Harbor Light Drop-In Clinic in East Oakland. When a patient is seen, a navigator can begin the same day: helping them apply for Medi-Cal, CalFresh and disability benefits, and working toward interim or permanent housing. Behavioural health clinicians on the van and at the clinic provide counselling, so mental health care is part of every visit rather than a separate referral. In 2025-26, 1,480 patients worked with a navigator. Because 38% of our patients have a serious mental illness diagnosis, this continuity matters: care is never conditional on sobriety or housing readiness.

questions.prompt: What outcomes did your programme achieve in the past year?
questions.answer: In 2025-26, 418 patients moved into interim or permanent housing with a peer navigator's help, and 1,290 patients were enrolled in Medi-Cal, CalFresh or disability benefits. Among patients with moderate or severe depression (PHQ-9 of 10 or more) who attended three or more counselling visits, 62% improved by 5 points or more. Emergency room visits among navigated patients fell 31% in the six months after enrolment. We track clinical data in our electronic health record and housing and benefits data in our navigator case-management database, and report both to our board quarterly.

program_report.title: Programme Progress Report: August 1 – September 30, 2026
program_report.content:
# Programme Progress Report: August 1 – September 30, 2026

## Street Medicine Van — Pacific Crest Health Foundation grant ($85,000)

In the first two months of the grant, the Street Medicine Van ran 5 days a week at all 14 regular stops in Oakland, Berkeley, Hayward and San Leandro, on schedule with our plan.

## Activity to date
- 1,190 van visits with 760 unique patients.
- 230 wound care visits and 410 medication refills.
- 165 patients received brief counselling from the van's behavioural health clinician.
- 128 patients were referred to a peer navigator; 47 of them have already been enrolled in Medi-Cal, CalFresh or disability benefits.

## Clinical outcomes to date
- Of 214 van patients with hypertension seen in the period, 55% had blood pressure under 140/90 at their last visit (organisation-wide in 2025-26: 58%).

## Challenges
The van was off the road for three days in September for brake repairs; we added a Saturday visit to the Hayward stop to make up the missed visits.

## Patient voice
"They remembered my name and my medication. I didn't have to start over." — Patient, San Leandro stop

## Spending to date
$14,150 of $85,000 spent (17%): $11,300 nurse practitioner time and $2,850 medical supplies, in line with the approved budget.

program_report.title: Programme Progress Report: June 1 – September 30, 2026
program_report.content:
# Programme Progress Report: June 1 – September 30, 2026

## Peer Navigator Programme — Estuary Housing Stability Fund grant ($120,000)

During the first four months of the grant, our 12 peer navigators, all with lived experience of homelessness, worked alongside clinicians on the Street Medicine Van and at the Harbor Light Drop-In Clinic in East Oakland.

## Participants and outcomes to date
- 590 patients worked with a peer navigator (on track for our annual total of about 1,480).
- 141 patients moved into interim or permanent housing: 96 into interim housing and 45 into permanent housing.
- 420 patients were enrolled in Medi-Cal, CalFresh or disability benefits.
- Emergency room use among navigated patients is measured six months after enrolment; first results will appear in the final report.

## Staffing
All 12 navigator positions stayed filled. Two new navigators completed our harm reduction and benefits training in July.

## Participant voice
"My navigator had been where I was. She sat with me through every form until I had keys." — Participant, Oakland

## Spending to date
$40,000 of $120,000 spent (33%) on peer navigator salaries and training, in line with the approved budget.

## Next steps
Tracking is done in our navigator case-management database and reported to the board quarterly; we will add a monthly housing-retention check for patients placed since June.
